title: Sain the barber
hook: Sain's aarti offers incense, lamp and ghee, then his whole self (Dhanasri, Sain, ang 695)

segments.voice: Yesterday, aarta: lentils, flour and a cow, asked for plainly at the Lord's door. Today, on the same page, a barber lights a lamp.

How close do you let a stranger come to your face with a blade? A barber's day is small, careful movements an inch from someone's throat. Trust is the whole job. Tradition remembers Sain as a barber, and on the same page of the Guru Granth Sahib as Dhanna's grocery list, he left a hymn of worship: an aarti, the lamp ceremony, with incense and flame. But by the end, what he offers isn't on the tray.
screen: `A BLADE NEAR THE FACE.` → `A BARBER'S CAREFUL HANDS.` → `AN AARTI ON THE SAME PAGE.`

segments.voice: Aarti, in Indian worship, is the waving of a lamp before the divine, often with incense and a lamp fed with ghee, clarified butter. Sain's hymn, in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 695, opens right there. In paraphrase: with incense, lamp and ghee I make ready the aarti. And in the next breath: I am a sacrifice to the Lord. Vaarne jaau, in the Gurmukhi: I give myself over. The tray is set, but the offering is the person holding it. The refrain is pure celebration: joy to the Lord, joy every day to the Sovereign King. Then Sain looks at the lamp again. The finest lamp, the purest wick, he sings, and turns to the Lord: You are the Immaculate One. As if the true flame isn't the one in his hand. Then a surprise: he names a teacher. Ramanand, he says, knows the devotion of the Lord, and speaks of the Lord as perfect, supreme bliss. Ramanand's own hymn comes in a few days. The close: worship the Lord, the supreme bliss, who carries you across the frightening sea. Tradition tells a story about Sain, retold by the Sikh poet Bhai Gurdas: once he stayed so long with holy people that he missed his duty at the king's court, and the Lord came in his form and served the king in his place. Whatever you make of the story, it fits the hymn: the barber's work and the barber's worship are one offering.
screen: `INCENSE, LAMP AND GHEE.` · `VAARNE JAAU: I GIVE MYSELF.` · `YOU ARE THE TRUE FLAME.` · then, large: `THE WORK AND THE WORSHIP, ONE OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Picture what your hands will do today, emails, meals, a shift, a diaper, a classroom, and see its tools the way Sain had scissors and comb. Quietly offer the work itself, done carefully, as your aarti, whether you call it that or not. If you pray, let Waheguru ride each breath out.
Aarti. The lamp ceremony of worship, incense and ghee on the tray, until Sain turns himself into the offering: I am a sacrifice to the Lord.
Your line: the barber's aarti. Scissors and comb belong on the tray too. That's day seven hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Sain's aarti is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teaching counts honest work, kirat, as part of a devoted life.

chat.says: There's a barber in the Guru Granth Sahib? What did he offer?
options: Sain readied incense, lamp and ghee, then offered himself: I am a sacrifice to the Lord.
Sain offered free haircuts to the Gurus, and that service is his whole hymn.
Sain offered a golden lamp, saying the finest lamp is what pleases the Lord.
chat.meaning: Sain's aarti on Ang 695 sets out incense, lamp and ghee, then says vaarne jaau, I give myself over: he becomes the offering.

aarti.meaning: worship with a waved lamp, incense and ghee

Vaarne jaau.meaning: I give myself over; I am a sacrifice

Ramanand.meaning: a teacher of devotion whose hymn is in the Granth

Bhai Gurdas.meaning: a Sikh poet whose verses explain the Gurus' teaching

Gurmukhi.meaning: the script the Guru Granth Sahib is written in

sources.ref: Dhanasri, Sain (dhoop deep ghrit saaj aartee), Ang 695

notes: Hymn paraphrased from memory (dhoop deep ghrit saaj aartee; vaarne jaau kamlaa patee; mangla har mangla; ootam deearaa nirmal baatee; raamaa bhagat raamaanand jaanai; sain bhanai bhaj paramaanande). 'Kamlaa patee' (Lord of Lakshmi) is rendered simply as 'the Lord'. Please check.
The Sain story (the Lord serving the king in his form) is attributed to Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 10; confirm the vaar and pauri (possibly 10.16).
Sikh practice around lamp-waving aarti varies and is deliberately not described; a Keeper may want a line on how Sikhs sing aarti hymns (e.g. in the evening).
Background on aarti (lamp, incense, ghee) is general description of Indian worship.
